Exclusive Lock ($X$): Read-write lock mode. Only one transaction can hold an exclusive lock on $Q$ at any given moment ($X-S$ and $X-X$ are strictly incompatible). Lock Compatibility Matrix: Requested \ Held Shared ($S$) Exclusive ($X$) Shared ($S$) Compatible (True) Incompatible (False) Exclusive ($X$) Incompatible (False) Incompatible (False) 2. Two-Phase Locking (2PL) Protocol: The basic 2PL protocol guarantees conflict serializability by requiring every transaction to separate its lock operations into two distinct, non-overlapping phases: Phase 1: Growing (Expanding) Phase: The transaction acquires new locks as needed and may upgrade locks ($S \to X$). It cannot release any lock under any circumstances. Lock Point: The exact instant when the transaction acquires its final lock (reaches peak lock count). The chronological order of lock points across transactions dictates their exact conflict serialization order. Phase 2: Shrinking (Contracting) Phase: The transaction releases held locks and may downgrade locks ($X \to S$). It cannot acquire any new locks once this phase begins. Serializability Guarantee: Because transactions never acquire new locks after releasing an earlier lock, no circular data item dependencies can be created, proving that 2PL guarantees conflict serializability.

title: Compare strict and rigorous two-phase locking with the help of an example, and state the benefits of each.
chunks: Strict 2PL and Rigorous 2PL are specialized variants of the Two-Phase Locking protocol that enforce stronger guarantees than basic 2PL. 1. Strict Two-Phase Locking (Strict 2PL): Rule: In addition to basic 2PL rules, a transaction must hold all its exclusive ($X$) locks until it terminates (commits or aborts). Shared ($S$) locks can be released during the shrinking phase before commit. Benefits: Guarantees recoverable and cascadeless schedules (prevents dirty reads), simplifying transaction rollback without cascading aborts. Allows concurrent reads to proceed earlier when shared locks are released. 2. Rigorous Two-Phase Locking (Rigorous 2PL): Rule: A transaction must hold all locks (both Shared $S$ and Exclusive $X$) until it terminates (commits or aborts). The shrinking phase collapses to the commit/abort point. Benefits: Guarantees strict serializability. Transactions can be serialized in the exact order in which they commit, making schedule analysis and replication coordination straightforward. 3. Comparative Example Schedule: Consider transaction $T_1$ needing to read $A$ and update $B$, and transaction $T_2$ needing to read $A$: Under Strict 2PL: $T_1$ acquires $S(A)$ and $X(B)$. After reading $A$, $T_1$ can release $S(A)$ early. $T_2$ can immediately acquire $S(A)$ and read $A$ before $T_1$ commits. However, $T_1$ retains $X(B)$ until commit. Under Rigorous 2PL: $T_1$

acquires $S(A)$ and $X(B)$. $T_1$ cannot release $S(A)$ until it commits. $T_2$ must wait if it needs an exclusive lock, ensuring strict chronological locking isolation. Dimension Strict 2PL Rigorous 2PL X-locks held until Commit / Abort Commit / Abort S-locks held until Can release in shrinking phase Commit / Abort Concurrency Level Higher (early S-lock release) Lower (locks held longer) Commit Ordering May differ from lock point Identical to commit order

title: Explain the architecture of a data warehouse (data sources, staging area, warehouse and presentation layer), describe the ETL process and state the role of data marts.
chunks: A Data Warehouse (DW) is a subject-oriented, integrated, time-variant, and non-volatile collection of corporate data structured for management decision-support analysis. 1. Architectural Layers: Data Sources: Operational transactional databases (OLTP), enterprise ERP and CRM systems, flat log files, web clickstreams, and third-party APIs. Staging Area: An intermediate holding and processing area where incoming data is extracted, sanitized, validated, and normalized before warehouse insertion, isolating production OLTP systems from query load. Warehouse (Enterprise Storage): The central repository storing integrated historical and atomic granular data organized according to enterprise-wide relational or dimensional data models. Presentation Layer: Front-end client applications providing reporting dashboards, OLAP multidimensional cubes, data visualization, and predictive data mining tools. Metadata Repository: Maintains administrative schemas, ETL business rules, transformation lineage, and indexing definitions, serving as the system directory across all warehouse components. 2. The ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) Process: Extract: Captures changed data (CDC) from heterogeneous relational databases, legacy systems, and unstructured files without interrupting live transaction processing. Transform: Performs critical data cleansing (handling null values and duplicates), standardizing disparate formats (e.g., converting dates to ISO standard, harmonizing currency codes), joining reference data, and generating artificial surrogate primary keys. Load: Executes bulk insertions of curated records into the target warehouse fact

and dimension tables during scheduled batch loading windows. 3. Role of Data Marts: A data mart is a departmental, highly focused subset of the warehouse customized for specific business units (such as Marketing, Finance, or Logistics). By structuring data into dedicated star or snowflake schemas, data marts deliver accelerated query performance, tighter security isolation, and tailored analytics without traversing the massive enterprise warehouse.

title: Why is two-phase locking (mostly strict 2PL) used in commercial DBMSs? Show with an example schedule that it can still cause deadlock, and write its other drawbacks.
chunks: Commercial database engines (such as Oracle, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server) overwhelmingly implement Strict Two-Phase Locking (Strict 2PL) as their primary concurrency control protocol. 1. Why Commercial DBMSs Adopt Strict 2PL: Guarantees Serializability: Like basic 2PL, it mathematically guarantees that all concurrent interleaved schedules are conflict serializable. Eliminates Cascading Aborts: By holding exclusive ($X$) locks until commit, transactions never write data that others read uncommitted; schedules are strictly cascadeless and recoverable. Simple Crash Recovery: Transaction rollback requires only undoing before-images without inspecting or aborting other transactions. 2. Deadlock Schedule Example under Strict 2PL: Strict 2PL does not prevent deadlocks. Consider two transactions $T_1$ and $T_2$ accessing data items $A$ and $B$: $T_1$ acquires $X(A)$ and writes to $A$. $T_2$ acquires $X(B)$ and writes to $B$. $T_1$ requests $X(B)$: since $T_2$ holds $X(B)$ until commit, $T_1$ must wait for $T_2$. $T_2$ requests $X(A)$: since $T_1$ holds $X(A)$ until commit, $T_2$ must wait for $T_1$. Both transactions hold resources while waiting for each other ($T_1 \to T_2 \to T_1$), creating a mutual deadlock that requires DBMS intervention. 3. Drawbacks of Two-Phase Locking: Deadlock Overhead: Systems must dedicate CPU cycles to maintain wait-for graphs, run cycle-detection routines, and abort/restart victims. Reduced Concurrency & Lock

Convoying: Long-running write transactions holding exclusive locks stall all subsequent readers and writers, degrading multi-user throughput. Lock Maintenance Cost: Allocating, updating, and hashing lock table entries adds memory consumption and lock manager processing latency. Phantom Anomalies: Tuple-level 2PL cannot stop phantom inserts into range queries unless expensive predicate/index-range locking is used.

title: Explain the deadlock prevention schemes Wait-Die and Wound-Wait with examples.
chunks: Deadlock prevention protocols use transaction timestamps to decide whether a requesting transaction should wait or abort when a resource conflict occurs. Monotonic timestamp $TS(T_i)$ is assigned when transaction $T_i$ begins (smaller timestamp implies older transaction). Suppose transaction $T_i$ requests a lock held by transaction $T_j$: 1. Wait-Die Scheme (Non-Preemptive): Older requests from Younger ($TS(T_i) < TS(T_j)$): $T_i$ is allowed to wait . Younger requests from Older ($TS(T_i) > TS(T_j)$): $T_i$ dies (aborts) and restarts with its original timestamp. Rule Summary: 'Old waits, young dies.' Locks are never preemptively stolen. Example: Let $TS(T_1)=10$ (older) and $TS(T_2)=20$ (younger). If $T_1$ requests a lock held by $T_2$, $T_1$ waits. If $T_2$ requests a lock held by $T_1$, $T_2$ dies and restarts. 2. Wound-Wait Scheme (Preemptive): Older requests from Younger ($TS(T_i) < TS(T_j)$): $T_i$ wounds $T_j$; $T_j$ is preempted, aborted, and rolls back, releasing its lock to $T_i$. $T_j$ restarts with its original timestamp. Younger requests from Older ($TS(T_i) > TS(T_j)$): $T_i$ is allowed to wait . Rule Summary: 'Old wounds, young waits.' Younger transactions are preempted by older ones. Example: With $TS(T_1)=10$ and $TS(T_2)=20$, if $T_1$ requests a lock held by $T_2$, $T_1$ preempts ($T_2$ is aborted). If $T_2$ requests a lock held

by $T_1$, $T_2$ waits. 3. Key Comparison: Metric Wait-Die Wound-Wait Preemption Non-preemptive Preemptive Number of Aborts High (young transactions die repeatedly) Fewer aborts; locks granted quickly to old Starvation Avoided (retains original timestamp) Avoided (retains original timestamp) Starvation Freedom Guarantee: In both schemes, when an aborted transaction restarts, it keeps its original starting timestamp. Thus, as time passes, the transaction becomes progressively older relative to new transactions, guaranteeing that it eventually becomes the oldest active transaction and runs to completion without ever dying again.

title: Construct a B+ tree in which every node can hold at most 3 keys (a maximum of 4 child pointers) by inserting the keys 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60 and 70 in the given order. Show the tree after every node split and state two advantages of a B+ tree over a B-tree.
chunks: Node Specification: Max keys $M = 3$, maximum child pointers $P = 4$. A node splits when the number of keys reaches 4. Step-by-Step Construction: Insert 10, 20, 30: All fit in the single root leaf node: [10, 20, 30] . Insert 40 (Split 1): Node overflows to [10, 20, 30, 40] . In a B+ tree leaf split, the middle key (index $\lceil 4/2 \rceil = 2$, key 30) is copied up to the parent. Left leaf keeps [10, 20] , right leaf keeps [30, 40] with a leaf sibling pointer. New root becomes [30] . Insert 50: Placed into right leaf: [30, 40, 50] . Tree valid. Insert 60 (Split 2): Right leaf overflows to [30, 40, 50, 60] . Leaf splits: left leaf retains [30, 40] , right leaf gets [50, 60] , and key 50 is copied up to root. Root now contains keys [30, 50] . Insert 70: Placed into rightmost leaf: [50, 60, 70] . Node is full but does not exceed 3 keys. Two Distinct Advantages of a B+ Tree over a Standard B-Tree: Extremely Fast Sequential Range Queries: In a B+ tree, all leaf nodes are linked into a continuous linked list.

Range queries execute by jumping to the start key via root search and simply scanning linearly across leaf sibling pointers, completely avoiding expensive in-order tree traversals required by B-trees. Higher Fanout and Lower Tree Height: Internal nodes in a B+ tree store only search keys and child pointers without actual data records. Consequently, each fixed-size disk page fits significantly more branch pointers (higher fanout), making the tree shallower and drastically reducing the number of disk I/O operations required for lookups.

title: A static hash file uses the hash function h(k) = k mod 5. Each bucket holds at most 2 records and overflow is handled by chaining. Insert the keys 5, 12, 21, 9, 17, 14, 8, 33, 22 and 7 in the given order and show the final contents of each bucket. Also explain how extendible hashing avoids long overflow chains. 5 Sr. No. Question Marks 120 A retail chain wants to analyse its sales by store, product and month. (i) Design a star schema with one fact table and suitable dimension tables. (ii) Explain the OLAP operations roll -up, drill-down and slice with an example from this schema. (iii) Analyse how the OLAP workload on this warehouse differs from the OLTP workload of the stores' billing systems.
chunks: Part 1: Static Hashing ($h(k) = k \bmod 5$, Bucket Capacity = 2, Chaining): $k=5: 5 \bmod 5 = 0 \to$ Bucket 0: [5] $k=12: 12 \bmod 5 = 2 \to$ Bucket 2: [12] $k=21: 21 \bmod 5 = 1 \to$ Bucket 1: [21] $k=9: 9 \bmod 5 = 4 \to$ Bucket 4: [9] $k=17: 17 \bmod 5 = 2 \to$ Bucket 2: [12, 17] (Full) $k=14: 14 \bmod 5 = 4 \to$ Bucket 4: [9, 14] (Full) $k=8: 8 \bmod 5 = 3 \to$ Bucket 3: [8] $k=33: 33 \bmod 5 = 3 \to$ Bucket 3: [8, 33] (Full) $k=22: 22 \bmod 5 = 2 \to$ Bucket 2 overflows $\to$ Chained Overflow Block: [22] $k=7: 7 \bmod 5 = 2 \to$ Bucket 2 overflow chain: [22, 7] Final Bucket Contents: Bucket 0: [5] ; Bucket 1: [21] ; Bucket 2: Primary [12, 17] $\to$ Chained Overflow [22, 7] ; Bucket 3: [8, 33] ; Bucket 4: [9, 14] . How Extendible Hashing Avoids Long Chains: Extendible hashing uses a dynamic directory with global and local depth. When a bucket overflows, only that specific bucket splits, doubling its local depth. If local depth exceeds global depth, the directory doubles. Records

are redistributed using additional hash bits, preventing sequential linear overflow search degradation. Part 2: Retail Star Schema & OLAP Workload: Star Schema Design: Central fact table Sales_Fact with measures ( quantity_sold , total_revenue ) and foreign keys ( store_id , product_id , time_id ), surrounded by dimension tables Store_Dim (location, city), Product_Dim (category, brand), and Time_Dim (day, month, quarter, year). OLAP Operations: Roll-up: Aggregates sales from Month to Year level. Drill-down: De-aggregates sales from Product Category down to individual Item. Slice: Filters sales for a single store (e.g., store_id = 'Store_101' ). OLAP vs. OLTP Workload: Store billing (OLTP) executes frequent, short, write-intensive ACID transactions with normalized schemas. The warehouse (OLAP) executes long-running, read-mostly, complex multi-table analytical aggregations over millions of denormalized historical records.

title: Differentiate between fragmentation and replication in a distributed database.
chunks: The core differences between fragmentation and replication in distributed databases are: Fragmentation: Divides a logical relation into non-overlapping sub-relations (horizontal rows, vertical columns, or hybrid) distributed across different sites without data duplication. Replication: Stores redundant full copies of a relation or fragment at two or more geographically distributed network sites to enhance availability and read locality.

title: State any two advantages and one drawback of data replication in a distributed database.
chunks: Data replication in distributed databases offers significant benefits and distinct trade-offs: Advantage 1 (High Availability): If a node holding data crashes, queries are transparently serviced by surviving replicas without downtime. Advantage 2 (Fast Read Performance): Read operations execute locally at the nearest replica site, eliminating wide-area network latency. Drawback (Update Overhead): Every write must be synchronized across all replicas, requiring distributed consensus protocols that increase write latency.

title: Define an index in MongoDB and state why it is used.
chunks: An index in MongoDB is a specialized auxiliary data structure (implemented as a B-tree) that stores a small portion of a collection's document fields in an easily traversable, sorted order. Why it is used: Query Acceleration: Avoids expensive full collection scans ( COLLSCAN ) by allowing the query engine to rapidly locate documents ( IXSCAN ). Efficient Sorting: Fulfills sorted queries directly from the index order without memory-intensive sort operations.

title: What is the purpose of the _id field in a MongoDB document?
chunks: The _id field serves as the mandatory primary key for every document in a MongoDB collection, uniquely identifying it within that collection. Default Generation: If omitted during insertion, MongoDB automatically populates _id with a unique 12-byte ObjectId (composed of timestamp, machine identifier, process ID, and incrementing counter). Unique Index: MongoDB automatically builds and maintains a unique index on _id , ensuring fast document lookups and preventing duplicate keys.

title: State the CAP theorem and name its three properties.
chunks: Brewer's CAP Theorem states that any distributed data store can simultaneously guarantee at most two out of three properties in the presence of network partitions. Its three core properties are: Consistency (C): Every read receives the most recent write or an error. Availability (A): Every non-failing node returns a non-error response for every request (without guaranteeing latest data). Partition Tolerance (P): The system continues to operate despite arbitrary network message losses or node network isolations.

title: What is a replica set in MongoDB?
chunks: A replica set in MongoDB is a cluster of mongod processes that maintain identical data copies to provide high availability and automatic failover. Primary Node: Exactly one primary receives all write operations, recording modifications in its replication operation log ( oplog ). Secondary Nodes: Multiple secondaries continuously replicate the primary's oplog and apply operations asynchronously. If the primary fails, secondaries elect a new primary via consensus.

title: Define sharding and state why it is used in MongoDB.
chunks: Sharding is a method for distributing data horizontally across multiple machines or clusters using a designated partition field known as a shard key . Why it is used in MongoDB: Horizontal Scalability (Scale-Out): Overcomes the hardware limits (RAM, CPU, disk I/O) of a single server by adding affordable commodity servers. Throughput Distribution: Partitions massive data sets and splits high-volume read/write query loads across independent shard servers.

title: Explain the main types of NoSQL databases and give one example product for each type.
chunks: NoSQL databases diverge from relational models by adopting non-tabular, flexible storage architectures: Key-Value Store: Stores data as associative arrays of unique keys paired with arbitrary binary values. Highly optimized for simple $O(1)$ lookups and session caches. Example: Redis , Amazon DynamoDB. Document-Oriented Database: Stores semi-structured data as self-describing BSON/JSON documents with nested objects and arrays, eliminating fixed relational schemas. Example: MongoDB , Couchbase. Column-Family (Wide-Column) Store: Organizes data into columns grouped into column families rather than rows, enabling high compression and massive analytical read throughput. Example: Apache Cassandra , Apache HBase. Graph Database: Represents data as nodes (entities) and edges (explicit relationships) with key-value properties, designed for complex network traversals without recursive relational joins. Example: Neo4j , Amazon Neptune.

title: Describe how data is organised in MongoDB into databases, collections and documents, with an example.
chunks: MongoDB organizes data hierarchically into three structural levels: Database: The outermost container that manages a physical set of files on disk. A single MongoDB instance can host multiple independent databases (e.g., universityDB ). Collection: A group of related documents housed inside a database, analogous to a relational table. However, collections are schema-free : documents in a collection do not need identical fields. Document: The fundamental atomic unit of data, serialized and stored in Binary JSON (BSON). Each document contains field-value pairs supporting nested objects, arrays, and an immutable _id primary key. Hierarchical Example: // Inside database: universityDB, collection: students { "_id": ObjectId("64a1b2c3d4e5f67890123456"), "rollNo": 101, "name": "Alice", "dept": "CSE", "address": { "city": "Bengaluru", "pincode": 560001 }, "courses": ["DBMS", "OS", "Networks"] }

title: Define a distributed database. Give two advantages and two challenges of such systems.
chunks: A distributed database is a collection of multiple logically interrelated databases distributed across different physical locations connected via a computer network, managed by a centralized Distributed DBMS (DDBMS). Two Advantages: Local Autonomy & Improved Performance: Sites maintain control over local data, allowing frequently accessed local queries to execute with zero network delay. High Availability and Reliability: Data replication ensures that if one server or geographical site suffers a failure, surviving nodes continue processing requests without system outages. Two Challenges: Complexity of Distributed Transactions: Maintaining ACID properties requires complex multi-phase commit protocols (e.g., 2PC) that increase latency and deadlock vulnerabilities. Network Overhead and Security: Latency across wide-area communication links impacts throughput, while distributed network endpoints expand the surface area for security threats.

title: Define a cloud database. Discuss its advantages and limitations compared with an on -premise database.
chunks: A cloud database is a database service deployed, configured, and accessed through a cloud platform (e.g., AWS RDS, Google Cloud Spanner, MongoDB Atlas), typically delivered as Database-as-a-Service (DBaaS). Advantages over On-Premise Databases: Elastic Scalability: Compute and storage resources can be scaled up or out dynamically with a single click or API call to match workload spikes. Automated Administration: Routine maintenance (patching, automated backups, hardware provisioning, failover) is managed transparently by the cloud vendor. Cost Efficiency: Eliminates upfront capital expenditure for enterprise server hardware, utilizing an operational pay-as-you-go model. Limitations: Vendor Lock-in: Migrating proprietary configurations and stored procedures between different cloud providers is technically challenging and expensive. Data Sovereignty & Network Dependency: Sensitive corporate data must comply with geographic compliance regulations (GDPR/HIPAA), and database availability is bound to external internet connection stability.

title: A MongoDB collection employees contains documents of the form {empid, nam e, dept, salary}. Write queries to (i) find the employees working in 'IT' or 'HR' using the $in operator and (ii) find the employees earning more than 50000, sorted by salary in descending order.
chunks: Given the employees collection schema {empid, name, dept, salary} , the required MongoDB queries are: (i) Employees working in 'IT' or 'HR' using the $in operator: db.employees.find({ dept: { $in: ["IT", "HR"] } }); Explanation: The $in comparison operator performs an equality match against an array of specified literal values, selecting any document where dept is either 'IT' or 'HR'. (ii) Employees earning more than 50,000, sorted by salary descending: db.employees.find({ salary: { $gt: 50000 } }).sort({ salary: -1 }); Explanation: The $gt operator filters records having salary strictly greater than 50,000. Chaining .sort({ salary: -1 }) orders output in descending order (-1 denotes descending, 1 denotes ascending).

title: A MongoDB collection students contains documents of the form {rollNo, name, dept, age, marks}. Write queries to (i) find the students aged between 18 and 22 (inclusive) using $gte and $lte, (ii) display only the name and marks of students who scored above 75, and (iii) count the students of the 'CSE' department.
chunks: Given collection students with schema {rollNo, name, dept, age, marks} : (i) Students aged between 18 and 22 inclusive: db.students.find({ age: { $gte: 18, $lte: 22 } }); Explanation: Combines $gte (greater than or equal) and $lte (less than or equal) inside the age field object. (ii) Display only name and marks of students scoring above 75: db.students.find( { marks: { $gt: 75 } }, { name: 1, marks: 1, _id: 0 } ); Explanation: The second argument defines a projection document: 1 includes fields, while _id: 0 explicitly suppresses the default primary key. (iii) Count students in the 'CSE' department: db.students.countDocuments({ dept: "CSE" }); Explanation: countDocuments() returns the accurate scalar integer count of matching documents.

title: Choose the most suitable type of NoSQL database (key-value, document, column-family or graph) for each case and justify your choice: (i) caching of user login sessions, (ii) a product catalogue with varying attributes, and (iii) friend recommendations on a social network.
chunks: Selection and justification of NoSQL database types for each use case: (i) Caching of User Login Sessions: Key-Value Database (e.g., Redis). Justification: A session token acts as a unique primary key pointing to user state. In-memory key-value stores deliver sub-millisecond $O(1)$ read/write latency with native TTL key expiration for automatic session timeouts. (ii) Product Catalogue with Varying Attributes: Document Database (e.g., MongoDB). Justification: Products have radically diverse attributes (laptops have CPU/RAM, shoes have size/color). A document model supports polymorphic JSON schemas where documents define custom attributes without sparse, null-filled relational columns. (iii) Friend Recommendations on a Social Network: Graph Database (e.g., Neo4j). Justification: Social platforms rely on interconnected networks. Graph databases represent users as nodes and friendships as direct edges, executing multi-hop traversals in milliseconds without recursive SQL joins.

title: Explain the BASE properties of NoSQL databases and contrast them briefly with ACID.
chunks: The BASE model governs distributed NoSQL systems, prioritizing horizontal availability over strict relational consistency: Basically Available: The database system remains operational and accessible to clients at all times, even in the event of partial node or network partition failures. Soft State: System state may fluctuate or drift over time even without client interaction, due to asynchronous replica propagation models. Eventual Consistency: The system does not guarantee immediate consistency on every read, but guarantees that all replicas will eventually converge to identical states if no further updates occur. Contrast with ACID: Pessimistic vs. Optimistic: ACID enforces strict, immediate consistency and serializable isolation via pessimistic locking, causing operations to stall or fail during partitions. Availability Priority: BASE embraces optimistic, relaxed consistency to guarantee uninterrupted availability ($A$) and partition tolerance ($P$) across large distributed clusters.

title: Differentiate between structured, semi-structured and unstructured data with one example of each.
chunks: Data in modern information architectures is categorized into three structural paradigms: Structured Data: Conforms to a strict, predefined tabular schema with fixed columns, specific data types, and explicit relational keys. Easily queried and manipulated using standard SQL. Example: An RDBMS relational table (e.g., Employee(EmpID, Name, Salary, HireDate) ) or CSV spreadsheets. Semi-Structured Data: Does not conform to a rigid relational schema, but contains internal organizational markers, tags, or hierarchies that separate individual data elements. Example: JSON documents, XML files, or BSON records (e.g., {"name": "Alice", "skills": ["DBMS", "Java"]} ). Unstructured Data: Data that has no predefined conceptual schema, model, or internal organizational structure. Requires specialized AI/ML algorithms or full-text parsing to extract meaning. Example: Video files, MP3 audio recordings, satellite imagery, and free-form scanned medical PDF reports.

title: A MongoDB collection orders contains documents of the form {orderId, custId, status, amount}. Write an aggregation pipeline to find the total amount of 'Delivered' orders for each customer, sorted in descending order of the total. Explain the role of each stage used.
chunks: The MongoDB aggregation pipeline processes documents through a multi-stage data transformation sequence: db.orders.aggregate([ { $match: { status: "Delivered" } }, { $group: { _id: "$custId", totalAmount: { $sum: "$amount" } } }, { $sort: { totalAmount: -1 } } ]); Explanation of Pipeline Stages: Stage 1 ( $match ): Acts as an initial filter stage (analogous to SQL WHERE ). Passes only documents where status === "Delivered" to downstream stages, dramatically minimizing subsequent memory overhead. Stage 2 ( $group ): Groups the filtered stream by the customer identifier ( _id: "$custId" ) (analogous to SQL GROUP BY ). It computes the aggregated metric totalAmount using the accumulator operator $sum: "$amount" . Stage 3 ( $sort ): Reorders the grouped output documents in descending order of totalAmount (-1 indicates descending sort order, analogous to SQL ORDER BY totalAmount DESC ).

title: Differentiate between insertOne and insertMany, updateOne and updateMany, and deleteOne and deleteMany in MongoDB, giving a one-line command for each.
chunks: MongoDB distinguishes between single-document and multi-document CRUD methods: insertOne vs. insertMany: insertOne inserts a single document into the collection. db.users.insertOne({ name: "Alice", age: 21 }); insertMany inserts an array of multiple documents in a single atomic batch call. db.users.insertMany([{ name: "Bob" }, { name: "Carol" }]); updateOne vs. updateMany: updateOne updates only the first matching document encountered in the collection. db.users.updateOne({ name: "Alice" }, { $set: { age: 22 } }); updateMany updates all documents in the collection that satisfy the query filter. db.users.updateMany({ dept: "HR" }, { $inc: { salary: 2000 } }); deleteOne vs. deleteMany: deleteOne removes at most one document matching the specified criteria. db.users.deleteOne({ name: "Bob" }); deleteMany deletes every document satisfying the filter condition. db.users.deleteMany({ status: "inactive" });

title: Explain how an index improves query performance in MongoDB. Write commands to (i) create an ascending index on the field name of the collection students, (ii) create a compound index on dept (ascending) and cgpa (descending), and (iii) create a unique index on rollno.
chunks: An index creates an ordered auxiliary B-tree structure mapping indexed field values to their physical document locations (RecordID) on disk. Without an index, MongoDB executes a full collection scan ( COLLSCAN ), examining every document in memory. With an index, it performs an index scan ( IXSCAN ), jumping directly to matching keys in $O(\log N)$ time. Index Creation Commands: (i) Ascending index on field name : db.students.createIndex({ name: 1 }); Explanation: 1 specifies an ascending index order. (ii) Compound index on dept (ascending) and cgpa (descending): db.students.createIndex({ dept: 1, cgpa: -1 }); Explanation: Indexes multiple fields together, accelerating queries that filter on dept and sort by cgpa . (iii) Unique index on field rollno : db.students.createIndex({ rollno: 1 }, { unique: true }); Explanation: The { unique: true } constraint causes MongoDB to reject any insert or update with duplicate rollno values.

title: In a MongoDB collection students whose documents look like {rollno, n ame, dept, cgpa, skills: [...]}, write commands to (i) list the name and cgpa of 'CSE' students whose cgpa is above 8, (ii) add 0.2 to the cgpa of the student with rollno 12, and (iii) remove every student whose cgpa is below 5.
chunks: Given the MongoDB collection students with schema {rollno, name, dept, cgpa, skills: [...]} , the required CRUD operations and execution semantics are structured as follows: (i) List the name and cgpa of 'CSE' students whose cgpa is above 8: db.students.find( { dept: "CSE", cgpa: { $gt: 8 } }, { name: 1, cgpa: 1, _id: 0 } ); Explanation: The query filter applies an implicit logical AND across both conditions: dept: "CSE" and the comparison operator cgpa: { $gt: 8 } . The second argument defines the projection specification, where name: 1 and cgpa: 1 include those fields in the output, while _id: 0 explicitly suppresses the default primary key field. (ii) Add 0.2 to the cgpa of the student with rollno 12: db.students.updateOne( { rollno: 12 }, { $inc: { cgpa: 0.2 } } ); Explanation: updateOne() targets the first document matching { rollno: 12 } . The $inc field update operator atomically increments the numeric value of cgpa by 0.2. In MongoDB, single-document updates are strictly atomic, eliminating race conditions without requiring an explicit transaction block. (iii) Remove every student whose cgpa is below 5: db.students.deleteMany({ cgpa: { $lt: 5 } }); Explanation: deleteMany() removes all documents in

the collection that satisfy the filter condition { cgpa: { $lt: 5 } } , using the less-than operator $lt . It returns an acknowledged write result object displaying the exact count of deleted documents. Indexing Optimization Note: To ensure high performance at scale, creating a compound index with db.students.createIndex({ dept: 1, cgpa: -1 }) enables the query engine to execute query (i) as an index scan ( IXSCAN ) instead of scanning every document in memory ( COLLSCAN ).

title: A MongoDB collection employees stores documents of the form {empid, name, dept, salary}. Write queries to (i) fetch the employees of the 'HR' department, (ii) fetch the employees earning more than 40000 using the $gt operator, and (iii) show only the name and salary of all em ployees in ascending order of salary.
chunks: Given the collection employees storing documents of the structure {empid, name, dept, salary} , the required query operations and execution mechanics are formulated as follows: (i) Fetch the employees of the 'HR' department: db.employees.find({ dept: "HR" }); Explanation: Performs an exact equality match against the dept field, retrieving all documents where the department string equals 'HR'. If no projection document is supplied as the second parameter, MongoDB returns all document fields including _id , empid , name , and salary . (ii) Fetch the employees earning more than 40,000 using the $gt operator: db.employees.find({ salary: { $gt: 40000 } }); Explanation: Utilizes the comparison operator $gt (greater than) within the criteria to filter and return documents where the numeric salary attribute strictly exceeds 40,000. (iii) Show only the name and salary of all employees in ascending order of salary: db.employees.find( {}, { name: 1, salary: 1, _id: 0 } ).sort({ salary: 1 }); Explanation: An empty query document {} matches all records in the collection. The projection document { name: 1, salary: 1, _id: 0 } restricts output exclusively to name and salary , while suppressing the default _id field. Chaining the cursor modifier .sort({ salary: 1 }) sorts the

output in ascending order of salary (where 1 denotes ascending and -1 denotes descending). Memory & Index Considerations: In MongoDB, in-memory sort operations are capped at 32 MB of RAM. Creating an index on { salary: 1 } allows MongoDB to retrieve sorted documents directly from the index tree without loading the entire collection into memory or exceeding sort RAM limits.

title: A start-up e-commerce company must handle (i) customer orders and payments, (ii) a product catalogue in which products have widely differing attributes, and (iii) millions of daily click -stream events and product recommendations. For each requirement, analyse whether an RDBMS or a NoSQL store such as MongoDB is more suitable, considering schema flexibility, consistency, scalability and joins. 5 Sr. No. Question Marks 143 In a MongoDB collection products with documents of the form {productId, productName, category, price}, write queries to (i) find the products in the 'Electronics' or 'Furniture' category using the $or operator, (ii) find the products priced between 1000 and 5000 using $gte and $lte, and (iii) display only the productName of the five costliest products.
chunks: Part 1: E-Commerce Architectural Analysis: (i) Customer Orders & Payments: RDBMS (e.g., PostgreSQL). Justification: Financial ledgers require strict ACID guarantees, multi-table foreign key constraints, and serializable isolation to prevent double payments or lost inventory. Financial records require immediate consistency and complex relational joins across tables (Customers, Orders, Payments, Invoices) that RDBMS handles natively. (ii) Product Catalogue with Diverse Attributes: NoSQL Document Store (MongoDB). Justification: Products possess widely variable attributes (e.g., laptops have RAM/storage, shirts have size/fabric). Relational databases require hundreds of sparse, null-filled columns or complex Entity-Attribute-Value (EAV) tables that ruin join performance. MongoDB's dynamic BSON schema allows polymorphic documents to coexist naturally in a single collection. (iii) Clickstream Events & Recommendations: Distributed NoSQL / Column Store (e.g., Cassandra / Redis). Justification: High-velocity clickstream ingest produces massive write volumes (millions of clicks/sec) that exceed RDBMS vertical scale limits. Distributed NoSQL stores provide horizontal sharding, high write throughput, and linear scalability under relaxed BASE consistency. Requirement Chosen Engine Schema Consistency Scalability Orders & Payments RDBMS Rigid Tabular Immediate (ACID) Vertical (Scale-up) Product Catalog MongoDB Flexible BSON Document Atomic Horizontal (Sharding) Clickstreams NoSQL (Cassandra/Redis) Key-Value/Column Eventual (BASE) Linear Scale-out Part 2: MongoDB Queries on Collection products : (i) Products in 'Electronics' or

'Furniture' using $or : db.products.find({ $or: [ { category: "Electronics" }, { category: "Furniture" } ] }); (ii) Products priced between 1,000 and 5,000 inclusive: db.products.find({ price: { $gte: 1000, $lte: 5000 } }); (iii) Display only productName of the five costliest products: db.products.find( {}, { productName: 1, _id: 0 } ).sort({ price: -1 }).limit(5);

title: A social media platform produces about 5 TB of posts, images, videos and 'like' events every day. Analyse this scenario in terms of volume, velocity, variety and veracity, explain why a traditional RDBMS struggles with it, and recommend suitable Big Data/NoSQL databases, giving one reason for each.
chunks: 1. Analysis of the Scenario via Big Data 4Vs: Volume: Generating 5 TB of raw data daily equates to ~150 TB/month and petabytes over years, far exceeding single-node server storage capacities. Velocity: Millions of concurrent user actions (likes, comments, video streams) arrive every second, demanding sub-millisecond ingest write speeds and real-time feed updates. Variety: Data encompasses structured user account profiles, semi-structured JSON post threads, and massive unstructured binary media (MP4 videos, JPEG images). Veracity: High proportion of noisy, duplicated, or unverified interactions (spam bots, rapid double-clicks, corrupted network packets) that require filtering. 2. Why a Traditional RDBMS Struggles: Vertical Scaling Bottlenecks: Traditional RDBMSs scale vertically (bigger CPU/RAM on one machine). A single server cannot process 5 TB daily write IOPS. Rigid Relational Schemas: RDBMS cannot dynamically ingest polymorphic post formats or evolving video metadata without costly schema migrations and table locks. Lock Contention & Joins: Strict ACID row-level locking causes severe lock contention on hot records (celebrity posts), and recursive multi-table SQL joins across petabytes of rows crush query latency. 3. Recommended Big Data / NoSQL Architecture: In-Memory Key-Value Store (Redis): For real-time 'like' counters, trending hashtags, and user session tokens with sub-millisecond in-memory caching and atomic increments. Wide-Column Distributed

Store (Apache Cassandra): For activity timeline feeds and interaction audit logs; provides masterless distributed writes across clusters with linear horizontal scaling and zero single point of failure. Distributed Object Store (Amazon S3 / Ceph) + CDN: For massive unstructured video and image media files, while keeping lightweight metadata and CDN URLs in MongoDB. Architectural Paradigm: Modern social architectures utilize a Lambda Architecture , separating high-velocity ingestion (speed layer via Kafka/Cassandra) from long-term analytical batch processing (Hadoop/Spark) under eventual consistency.

title: A university stores student attendance, examination results, course registrations and feedback in a MongoDB collection students with documents of the form {rollno, name, attendance, marks, feedback: [...]}. Explain how MongoDB's flexible schema and document model suit such records better than fixed relational tables, and write queries to (i) find the students with attendance below 75, (ii) find the students with marks above 80, and (iii) find the students who satisfy both conditions.
chunks: 1. Architectural Suitability of MongoDB's Document Model: Elimination of Relational Joins: In an RDBMS, this scenario requires four normalized tables ( Students , Attendance , ExamMarks , Feedback ) connected via foreign keys, requiring expensive multi-table SQL joins. MongoDB nests attendance, marks, and an array of feedback subdocuments into a single document, retrieving complete student records in a single disk read. Polymorphic Schema Flexibility: Different academic departments have varying feedback templates, optional elective fields, and grading criteria. MongoDB's dynamic schema allows documents to store custom department fields without requiring schema alterations or creating sparse tables with null columns. Natural 1-to-Many Representation: The feedback: [...] array natively encapsulates embedded subdocuments (with instructor name, rating, comments), preserving document locality on disk. Document Schema Validation: MongoDB supports JSON Schema validation to enforce data integrity (e.g., verifying cgpa >= 0 and attendance <= 100 ) while retaining complete field flexibility. 2. MongoDB Queries: (i) Students with attendance below 75: db.students.find({ attendance: { $lt: 75 } }); Explanation: The $lt operator matches all student records whose attendance percentage is strictly under 75. (ii) Students with marks above 80: db.students.find({ marks: { $gt: 80 } }); Explanation: The $gt operator filters records where academic marks exceed

80. (iii) Students who satisfy both conditions (attendance < 75 AND marks > 80): db.students.find({ attendance: { $lt: 75 }, marks: { $gt: 80 } }); Explanation: Specifying comma-separated field criteria in a single query document enforces an implicit boolean AND condition, returning students with poor attendance who nevertheless achieved high marks.

title: A healthcare organisation collects patient records, medical reports, diagnostic images and real -time data from wearable devices. Analyse the challenges that such diverse, continuously generated data creates for a traditional relational database. Explain how MongoDB's flexible schema, sharding and replication help meet these challenges, and describe how the large diagnostic images can be stored (for example with GridFS or an object store with metadata kept in MongoDB), justifying your choice.
chunks: 1. Challenges for a Traditional Relational Database: Schema Rigidity: Medical reports and clinical lab tests vary wildly across specializations (cardiology, oncology). Enforcing rigid relational tables causes extensive schema bloat, dozens of null columns, and costly ALTER TABLE lockups. High-Velocity Time-Series Streaming: Continuous wearable telemetry (heart rate, SpO2) produces millions of timestamped write events per minute, overwhelming RDBMS single-server disk I/O and transaction logging. Large Binary Data Overhead: High-resolution medical imaging (MRI, CT scans in DICOM format, often 50 MB to 1 GB) stored as database BLOBs exhausts memory buffers, degrades backup speeds, and hampers query performance. 2. How MongoDB Addresses These Challenges: Flexible Schema: JSON/BSON document model naturally accommodates heterogeneous patient profiles, varying lab diagnostics, and dynamic doctor prescriptions. Sharding: Horizontally distributes streaming IoT wearable vitals across multiple shard nodes using a compound shard key (e.g., { patientId: 1, timestamp: 1 } ), balancing write throughput. Replication: Multi-node replica sets ensure 99.999% clinical availability, disaster recovery, and zero data loss during hardware failures. 3. Storing Diagnostic Images (Architecture & Justification): GridFS: MongoDB's specification for storing files exceeding the 16 MB document limit by automatically splitting binaries into 255 KB chunks across fs.files and fs.chunks collections. Recommended Approach (Hybrid Object Store

+ MongoDB): Store high-resolution binary DICOM image files in a dedicated cloud object store (e.g., Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage) and store rich clinical metadata (Patient ID, scan date, modality, S3 presigned URL, AI diagnosis tags) inside MongoDB. Justification: Cloud object stores offer lower per-gigabyte storage costs, native CDN integration for hospital workstations, and keep MongoDB working-set RAM lean and dedicated to high-speed clinical metadata indexing.

title: Analyse the suitability of MongoDB for (i) storing IoT sensor readings and (ii) a content management system of a news website. For each, justify your decision by discussing schema flexibility, scalability and consistency/transaction needs, and mention one more real-world application where MongoDB fits well.
chunks: MongoDB's document-oriented architecture provides compelling advantages across specific industry workloads: (i) IoT Sensor Readings: Schema Flexibility: Diverse sensors (temperature, vibration, pressure, GPS) produce disparate payload structures. MongoDB easily ingests varying JSON metrics without requiring rigid column definitions. Scalability: High-frequency telemetry streams are partitioned across clusters via horizontal sharding . Native time-series collections (specifying timeField and metaField ) optimize storage footprint through automated bucket compression and columnar disk layouts. Consistency & Transactions: IoT streams tolerate eventual consistency. Configurable write concerns (e.g., { w: 1 } ) maximize write throughput over strict multi-document serializability. Verdict: Highly Suitable for massive, append-only sensor telemetry. (ii) Content Management System (CMS) of a News Website: Schema Flexibility: News stories feature rich, evolving structures: varied multimedia embeds, editorial revision histories, author arrays, and tagging hierarchies. The document model represents an entire article and its comments natively in a single BSON document. Scalability: Breaking news generates massive read spikes. MongoDB handles high read volume via replica sets , directing queries to secondary nodes using nearest or secondaryPreferred read preferences. Consistency & Transactions: Publishing an article is an atomic, single-document write; MongoDB provides native single-document ACID transactions, satisfying editorial publishing requirements. Verdict: Extremely Well-Suited for high-read, semi-structured editorial content.

Additional Real-World Application: E-Commerce Product Catalog. E-commerce catalogs feature millions of products with wildly heterogeneous attributes (e.g., electronics, apparel, groceries). MongoDB stores polymorphic products within a single collection, supports fast multi-attribute compound indexing, and enables rapid catalog search without expensive SQL joins. Additionally, multikey indexes on embedded arrays enable instant filtering on multi-valued product tags (such as available sizes, colors, and technical specifications) without maintaining separate relational junction tables.

title: Explain replication in MongoDB with reference to the primary and secondary members of a replica set, the election of a new primary when the current primary fails, and write concern. State the benefits of replication.
chunks: Replication in MongoDB provides redundancy, high availability, and automated failover across distributed nodes. 1. Replica Set Architecture: Primary Member: Exactly one primary accepts all write operations, recording changes in a capped collection called the oplog (operations log) . Secondary Members: Secondaries continuously read the primary's oplog and apply operations asynchronously to replicate data state. They can serve read queries if configured. Arbiter (Optional): A lightweight voting-only member that holds no data, used solely to break election ties in clusters with even node counts. 2. Election of a New Primary: Members send heartbeat pings every 2 seconds. If secondaries receive no response from the primary within 10 seconds, an election is triggered. Secondaries nominate eligible members based on member priority and oplog recency; the node holding the most up-to-date oplog that wins a strict majority of votes becomes the new Primary. 3. Write Concern: Write concern specifies the level of acknowledgement requested from MongoDB for write operations: { w: 1 } : Acknowledged by Primary only (fast, but data could be lost if primary fails before replication). { w: "majority" } : Acknowledged only after the write is committed to a majority of replica set nodes, preventing rollback during failover. {

j: true } : Ensures the operation is written to on-disk journal before returning acknowledgement. 4. Benefits of Replication: Guarantees continuous 24/7 high availability, eliminates single points of failure, allows zero-downtime rolling maintenance/upgrades, and offloads heavy analytical read traffic from the primary node. Strong write concerns (such as w: 'majority' ) protect mission-critical applications against data rollbacks if a primary node suddenly experiences ungraceful hardware failure before replication completes.

title: A MongoDB collection students contains documents of the form {rollno, name, dept, cgpa, skills: [...]}. Write aggregation pipelines to (i) display the number of students in each department, (ii) display the departments whose average cgpa is greater than 7.5 along with that average, and (iii) display the number of students having each skill using $unwind.
chunks: The MongoDB Aggregation Framework transforms document streams through multi-stage pipelines to perform complex analytical data transformations: (i) Display the number of students in each department: db.students.aggregate([ { $group: { _id: "$dept", studentCount: { $sum: 1 } } } ]); Explanation: The $group stage groups documents by the dept field ( _id: "$dept" ). The accumulator expression { $sum: 1 } increments a counter by 1 for each document in the group, outputting the department name and total headcount. (ii) Display departments whose average cgpa is greater than 7.5 along with the average: db.students.aggregate([ { $group: { _id: "$dept", avgCgpa: { $avg: "$cgpa" } } }, { $match: { avgCgpa: { $gt: 7.5 } } } ]); Explanation: Stage 1 computes the average CGPA per department using { $avg: "$cgpa" } . Stage 2 applies a $match filter on the aggregated metric, acting like SQL HAVING avgCgpa > 7.5 to retain only qualifying departments. (iii) Display the number of students having each skill using $unwind : db.students.aggregate([ { $unwind: "$skills" }, { $group: { _id: "$skills", count: { $sum: 1 } } }, { $sort: { count: -1 } } ]); Explanation: $unwind deconstructs the skills array field, generating a separate

clone document for each array element. The subsequent $group stage groups by individual skill name and counts occurrences with { $sum: 1 } . Finally, $sort arranges skills in descending order of student popularity. Pipeline Performance Note: Each aggregation stage has a 100 MB RAM limit. For large collections, enabling { allowDiskUse: true } ensures that memory-intensive grouping and sorting stages can spill intermediate data to disk temporary files.

title: Analyse the trade-offs of the CAP theorem for a distributed database during a network partition. Using this analysis, justify whether a CP or an AP design is more suitable for (i) an online banking ledger and (ii) a social-media news feed, and explain how sharding and replication help a NoSQL system to scale.
chunks: 1. CAP Theorem Trade-Off Analysis during Network Partition: The CAP theorem states that a distributed system cannot simultaneously guarantee Consistency ($C$), Availability ($A$), and Partition Tolerance ($P$). Because physical network partitions ($P$) (cable cuts, packet loss, hardware switch failures) are unavoidable in distributed architectures, systems must choose between Consistency or Availability when a partition occurs: CP (Consistency + Partition Tolerance): Rejects the read/write request on the isolated partition to prevent stale or conflicting data, returning an error or timeout. Sacrifices Availability to preserve absolute mathematical correctness. AP (Availability + Partition Tolerance): Returns the locally available value (even if stale) and accepts writes locally. Sacrifices immediate Consistency to guarantee 100% Availability. 2. Application Justifications: (i) Online Banking Ledger: CP Design (e.g., Google Spanner, MongoDB with majority write concern). Justification: Financial ledgers require zero tolerance for dirty reads, phantom withdrawals, or double-spending. If a network partition prevents verifying account balances across branches, the system must abort the transaction rather than serve incorrect monetary balances. (ii) Social-Media News Feed: AP Design (e.g., Apache Cassandra, Amazon DynamoDB). Justification: User experience demands seamless, uninterrupted availability. If a user sees a friend's post or like count 5 seconds late due to a network partition, the business

impact is negligible compared to showing a broken error screen. 3. How Sharding and Replication Enable NoSQL Scaling: Sharding (Horizontal Scale-Out): Splits massive collections into disjoint ranges based on a shard key, distributing storage and write throughput across dozens of commodity servers. Replication (High Availability & Read Scaling): Maintains identical copies across nodes, eliminating single points of failure and distributing read query loads geographically.

Unit I: Intro & ER DBMS

Definition A Database Management System (DBMS) is software that interacts with end-users, applications, and the database itself to capture and analyze data. It allows users to create, read, update, and delete data in a database. Advantages over File-Processing Data Redundancy and Inconsistency: Centralizes data, eliminating duplicate files and ensuring updates propagate everywhere. Data Isolation: Applications do not need to know the physical structure of the data files. Integrity Problems: Allows defining explicit integrity constraints (e.g., account balance > 0). Security Problems: Offers fine-grained access control and user authorization. Concurrent Access: Manages simultaneous access securely, preventing anomalies. Data redundancy and data inconsistency

Definitions Data Redundancy: The unnecessary duplication of data in a database. (e.g., storing a student's address in both the Library and Department files). Data Inconsistency: A consequence of redundancy where different copies of the same data hold different values (e.g., address updated in Library but not Department). DBMS Solution A DBMS minimizes redundancy by storing a single, centralized copy of the data (Data Normalization). Because there is only one authoritative copy, inconsistency is inherently prevented. Give the difference between a database system and a file-based system

Differences Structure: DB systems store data in structured formats (tables/graphs); File systems store data in plain text/binary files. Data Independence: DB systems separate applications from data structure; File systems tightly couple applications to file formats. Querying: DB systems provide robust query languages (SQL); File systems require custom application code to extract data. Draw and explain the three-level (ANSI-SPARC) architecture of a DBMS

The Three Levels External Level (View Level): The highest level, describing only the part of the database relevant to a specific user group (hiding the rest). Conceptual Level (Logical Level): Describes what data is stored in the entire database and the relationships among those data. Used by DBAs. Internal Level (Physical Level): Describes exactly how the data is physically stored on disk (data structures, file organizations). Exam Tip: The primary objective of this architecture is to achieve Data Independence . Data abstraction

Definition Data abstraction is the process of hiding complex internal data structures and storage details from the user, presenting only a simplified, usable view of the data. Three Levels Physical Level: Hides the complexity of block structures, indexing, and bytes on disk. Logical Level: Hides physical storage but reveals entities, data types, and relationships. Developers interact here. View Level: Hides the entire logical schema except for specific fields the end-user is authorized to see (e.g., a teller seeing only names and balances). Terms schema and instance

Definition Schema: The overall logical design/blueprint of the database. It changes rarely. Instance: The snapshot of data residing in the database at a specific moment in time. It changes frequently. Importance This distinction is crucial for maintaining data independence—altering the schema (like adding a column) should not arbitrarily destroy the existing instances. Data independence

Definition Data independence is the ability to modify a schema definition in one level without affecting a schema definition in the next higher level. Types Physical Data Independence: Ability to modify the internal/physical schema without altering the conceptual schema. Example: Changing a file from sequential to a B+ tree index to improve performance; application code doesn't change. Logical Data Independence: Ability to modify the conceptual schema without altering the external schema (user views). Example: Splitting an Employee table into two normalized tables; the original view can be maintained using a SQL JOIN, shielding the frontend application. Who are the different types of database users

Types of Users Parametric (Naive) Users: End-users who interact via standard GUI applications without knowing SQL (e.g., Bank Tellers). Application Programmers: Software engineers who write the backend logic connecting to the DB. Sophisticated Users: Analysts who interact directly with the DB using SQL queries to generate reports. Database Administrators (DBA): IT professionals who manage security, schemas, and performance tuning. List the responsibilities of a Database Administrator (DBA)

Responsibilities Schema definition and modification. Defining storage structures and access methods (indexing). Granting user authority and managing access security. Routine maintenance, database backups, and performance monitoring. Hierarchical, network, relational and object-oriented data models

Comparison Hierarchical: Data organized in a tree structure (1:N relationships). Fast but inflexible; requires navigating rigid pointers. Network: Data organized in a graph (M:N relationships allowed). Highly complex and difficult to maintain. Relational: Data organized in 2D tables (relations). Uses declarative SQL. Extremely flexible and mathematically sound. Object-Oriented: Data stored as objects with methods, matching OOP languages. Best for complex data (e.g., CAD/CAM). Most Widely Used The Relational Model is most widely used today due to its simplicity, robust theoretical foundation (normalization), and standard interface (SQL) which provides unparalleled data independence. Advantages of the relational model over the other data models

Advantages Simplicity: Uses a simple tabular structure (rows and columns) that is easy to understand compared to complex graph/tree pointers. Flexibility: Supports ad-hoc querying using standard SQL. Data Independence: Strong separation between logical representation and physical storage. Terms super key, candidate key, primary key and foreign key

Explanation Super Key: Any combination of columns that uniquely identifies a row. (e.g., StudentID + Name ) Candidate Key: A minimal super key; it uniquely identifies a row with no unnecessary columns. (e.g., StudentID or Email ) Primary Key: The specific candidate key chosen to identify rows. Cannot be NULL. (e.g., StudentID ) Foreign Key: A column that refers to the primary key of another table, enforcing referential integrity. (e.g., Dept_ID in a Student table referencing the Department table) Integrity constraints in a relational model

Definition Integrity constraints are rules applied to a database to ensure the data is accurate, consistent, and valid. The Four Constraints Domain Constraint: Restricts the values a column can hold to a valid set (e.g., Age must be a positive integer). Key Constraint: Ensures that candidate/primary keys are completely unique for every row. Entity Integrity: States that no part of a Primary Key can be NULL, because a NULL value cannot uniquely identify a row. Referential Integrity: States that if a foreign key exists in a relation, its value must either match a primary key value in the referenced relation or be NULL. (e.g., You cannot enroll a student in a non-existent Course_ID). E-R model

Definition The Entity-Relationship (E-R) model is a high-level conceptual data model that visually represents entities (objects) and the relationships between them. Notations Rectangle: Entity sets Ellipse: Attributes Diamond: Relationship sets Lines: Link attributes to entities and entities to relationships Entity, entity set, attribute and relationship, and illustrate each

Definitions Entity: A real-world object with independent existence (e.g., a specific student). Entity Set: A collection of similar entities (e.g., all Students). Attribute: A property describing an entity (e.g., Name, Age). Relationship: An association among two or more entities (e.g., Student Enroll Course). Different types of attributes, simple, composite, derived, multivalued and key attribute,

Attribute Types Simple: Indivisible atomic values (e.g., Gender ). Composite: Can be broken down into sub-parts (e.g., Name into First Name, Last Name). Derived: Calculated from other attributes; not physically stored (e.g., Age derived from DOB). Multivalued: Can hold multiple values for a single entity (e.g., Phone_Numbers ). Key: Uniquely identifies the entity (e.g., Roll_No ). Different types of relationships that can exist between two entities

Cardinality Ratios One-to-One (1:1): One entity in A is associated with at most one in B. (e.g., Department 1:1 Manager). One-to-Many (1:N): One entity in A is associated with many in B. (e.g., Department 1:N Employees). Many-to-Many (M:N): Many entities in A associated with many in B. (e.g., Student M:N Course). Weak entity set

Definition A weak entity set lacks sufficient attributes to form a primary key. It depends on a strong entity (identifying owner) and uses the owner's key plus its own partial key to identify rows. Example A Dependent (spouse/child) of an Employee. The dependent is identified by combining their Name (partial key) with the owner's Employee ID. Unary, binary and ternary relationships

Degrees of Relationships Unary (Degree 1): Relationship between instances of a single entity set (e.g., Employee Manages Employee). Binary (Degree 2): Relationship between two entity sets (e.g., Student Takes Course). Ternary (Degree 3): Relationship connecting three entity sets simultaneously (e.g., Supplier Supplies Part To Project). Exam Tip: A ternary relationship is not just three binary relationships; it represents a single fact involving all three entities together. Total participation and partial participation constraints in an E-R diagram

Differentiation Total Participation (Mandatory): Every entity MUST participate in at least one relationship. Indicated by a double line. (e.g., Every Employee must belong to a Department). Partial Participation (Optional): Only some entities may participate. Indicated by a single line. (e.g., Only some Employees are Managers of a Department). Generalization and specialization in the Extended E-R model

Specialization (Top-Down) The process of defining a set of subclasses from a single entity type (the superclass). It involves identifying characteristics that distinguish some entities in the set from others. Example: An Employee superclass can be specialized into Engineer , Manager , and Technician subclasses based on job role. Generalization (Bottom-Up) The reverse process of specialization. Multiple entity types with common attributes are synthesized into a single, generalized superclass. Example: Car and Truck entities share attributes like Vehicle_ID and Price, so they can be generalized into a Vehicle superclass. Overlapping and disjoint specialization

Disjoint Specialization An entity can be a member of at most one subclass of the specialization. Denoted by a 'd' in the circle. Example: An Employee can be either an Hourly_Employee or a Salaried_Employee , but never both at the same time. Overlapping Specialization An entity may be a member of more than one subclass of the specialization. Denoted by an 'o' in the circle. Example: A Person can simultaneously be an Alumnus and an Employee of a university. Aggregation in E-R modelling

Definition Aggregation is an abstraction where a relationship set (and its associated entities) is treated as a higher-level entity set. When is it required? The basic E-R model cannot express relationships among relationships. Aggregation is required when a relationship between two entities needs to participate in another relationship with a third entity. Example Consider Employee working on a Project . This forms the relationship Works_On . If we want to record the Manager who oversees this specific (Employee-Project) assignment, we aggregate Works_On into a single entity, and create a new relationship Manages between it and Manager . Mapping cardinality

Definition Mapping cardinality (or cardinality ratio) expresses the number of entities to which another entity can be associated via a relationship set. Types One-to-One (1:1): An entity in A is associated with at most one entity in B, and vice versa. One-to-Many (1:N): An entity in A is associated with any number of entities in B. An entity in B is associated with at most one entity in A. Many-to-One (N:1): An entity in A is associated with at most one entity in B. An entity in B is associated with any number of entities in A. Many-to-Many (M:N): An entity in A is associated with any number of entities in B, and vice versa. Functional dependency

Definition A functional dependency (FD) is a constraint between two sets of attributes in a relation. If A → B (A determines B), then for every valid instance of the relation, any two tuples that agree on the attribute A must also agree on the attribute B. Importance Functional dependencies are the theoretical bedrock of Normalization . They are used to specify constraints on data, discover candidate keys, and decompose relations to eliminate redundancy and update anomalies. Insertion, deletion and update anomalies

The Three Anomalies Update Anomaly: If data is stored redundantly, changing it in one row requires changing it in all rows. Missing one causes inconsistency (e.g., changing a department's location). Insertion Anomaly: The inability to add data to the database due to absence of other data (e.g., unable to add a new Department because it has no Employees yet, and Employee_ID is the primary key). Deletion Anomaly: The unintended loss of data when deleting a row (e.g., deleting the only employee in a department also deletes the department's information). How Normalization Helps Normalization resolves these by decomposing large, poorly structured tables into smaller, well-structured tables where each table represents a single logical theme or entity. By linking them with foreign keys, redundancy is eliminated, which inherently solves update, insertion, and deletion anomalies. Normalization

Definition Normalization is the process of organizing data to minimize redundancy and eliminate anomalies by dividing larger tables into smaller tables and defining relationships between them using functional dependencies. The Normal Forms First Normal Form (1NF): All attributes must be atomic (indivisible). No repeating groups or arrays allowed in a cell. Second Normal Form (2NF): Must be in 1NF, and all non-key attributes must be fully functionally dependent on the entire primary key. (Eliminates partial dependencies). Third Normal Form (3NF): Must be in 2NF, and no non-key attribute can be dependent on another non-key attribute. (Eliminates transitive dependencies: X → Y and Y → Z). BCNF

Definition Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF) requires that for every non-trivial functional dependency X → Y, X must be a super key. It is a stronger, stricter version of 3NF. Difference from 3NF 3NF allows a dependency X → Y where X is NOT a super key, provided that Y is a prime attribute (part of a candidate key). BCNF does not allow this exception. A table can be in 3NF but fail BCNF if it has overlapping candidate keys. Example Consider Relation(Student, Course, Instructor) . Keys are (Student, Course) and (Student, Instructor). FD: Instructor → Course . It is in 3NF because Course is a prime attribute. However, it violates BCNF because Instructor is not a super key. Write a short note on 4NF and 5NF,

Fourth Normal Form (4NF) Deals with Multi-valued Dependencies (MVD) . A table is in 4NF if it is in BCNF and contains no non-trivial multi-valued dependencies (where one attribute determines a set of values for another, independent of a third). Example: An Employee has multiple Skills and multiple Dependents. Storing them in one table creates massive redundancy. We split into (Emp, Skill) and (Emp, Dependent) . Fifth Normal Form (5NF) Deals with Join Dependencies . Also known as Project-Join Normal Form (PJNF). A table is in 5NF if it is in 4NF and cannot be decomposed into smaller tables without losing data (lossless join). It ensures that all join dependencies are implied by candidate keys. Lossless-join decomposition

Definition Lossless-join decomposition means that if a relation R is decomposed into R1 and R2, joining them back together via a Natural Join will yield the exact original relation R, without any missing rows (loss of data) or extra spurious rows (creation of invalid data). Condition The decomposition is lossless if the common attribute(s) between R1 and R2 form a super key for either R1 or R2. (i.e., R1 ∩ R2 → R1 OR R1 ∩ R2 → R2). Example Splitting Employee(ID, Name, Dept, Dept_Location) into Emp(ID, Name, Dept) and Department(Dept, Dept_Location) is lossless because their intersection, Dept , is a primary key for the Department table. Dependency-preserving decomposition and give a suitable example

Definition A decomposition is dependency-preserving if the union of the functional dependencies in the decomposed relations logically implies all the functional dependencies of the original relation. This ensures that updates can be checked for validity without joining the tables back together. Example Original Relation: R(A, B, C) Functional Dependencies (FDs): A → B, B → C Decomposition: R1(A, B) and R2(B, C). FDs in R1: A → B. FDs in R2: B → C. Since (A → B) ∪ (B → C) covers all original FDs, it is a dependency-preserving decomposition . Identifying Partial Dependencies Suppose the relation is R(StudentID, SubjectID, StudentName, Grade) . The primary key is (StudentID, SubjectID) . StudentID → StudentName (StudentName depends only on part of the key) — Partial Dependency StudentID, SubjectID → Grade (Grade depends on the whole key) — Full Dependency Decomposition into 2NF We split the table to remove the partial dependency: Student ( StudentID , StudentName) Enrollment ( StudentID, SubjectID , Grade) Both tables are now in 2NF as all non-prime attributes fully depend on their respective primary keys. Violation of 3NF Consider Employee(EmpID, Name, DeptID, DeptName) where EmpID is the primary key. Functional Dependencies: 1. EmpID → DeptID 2. DeptID → DeptName Because EmpID → DeptName through DeptID , this is a Transitive Dependency . 3NF forbids non-prime attributes depending on other non-prime attributes. Decomposition into 3NF We decompose the relation to separate the department details: Employee ( EmpID , Name, DeptID ) Department ( DeptID , DeptName) In the table below, each mentor teaches only one subject

Checking BCNF Relation: R(StudentID, Subject, Mentor) FDs: {StudentID, Subject} → Mentor , and Mentor → Subject (each mentor teaches one subject). Because Mentor → Subject exists, but Mentor is not a super key , the table violates BCNF (even though it is in 3NF since Subject is a prime attribute). BCNF Decomposition We must pull the violating determinant out into its own table: Mentor_Subject ( Mentor , Subject) Student_Mentor ( StudentID, Mentor ) Now all determinants are candidate keys. Table below stores a student's hobbies and the languages they know together, forcing every combination to be listed

Violation of 4NF Relation: R(StudentID, Hobby, Language) A student's hobbies are completely independent of the languages they speak. This creates two Multi-Valued Dependencies (MVDs) : StudentID ⟶ Hobby and StudentID ⟶ Language . Storing them together forces a Cartesian product (e.g., 2 hobbies × 3 languages = 6 rows for one student). Since 4NF forbids non-trivial MVDs, this violates 4NF. 4NF Decomposition Split into two tables to eliminate the Cartesian product: Student_Hobby ( StudentID, Hobby ) Student_Language ( StudentID, Language ) Given a relation R(A, B, C, D, E)

Computing {A, C} + Start with the base set: {A, C} Using A → B , add B. The set becomes {A, B, C} Using BC → D (we have both B and C), add D. The set becomes {A, B, C, D} Using D → E , add E. The set becomes {A, B, C, D, E} Conclusion Since the closure of {A, C} contains all the attributes of the relation R, {A, C} is a super key . Assuming no proper subset of {A, C} can determine all attributes, {A, C} is a Candidate Key . Consider the relation Student_Course(Roll_No, Course_ID, Course_Name, Instructor)

Analysis Primary Key: (Roll_No, Course_ID) The FD Course_ID → Course_Name is a Partial Dependency because Course_Name depends only on a part of the primary key (Course_ID), violating 2NF. 2NF Decomposition Course ( Course_ID , Course_Name) Student_Course ( Roll_No, Course_ID , Instructor) Now, both relations are in 2NF. Consider the relation Employee(Emp_ID, Emp_Name, Dept_ID, Dept_Name, Dept_Location)

Analysis Primary Key: Emp_ID . Since the key is a single attribute, there are no partial dependencies, so it is in 2NF . However, the FD Dept_ID → Dept_Name, Dept_Location creates a Transitive Dependency (Emp_ID → Dept_ID → Dept_Name). This violates 3NF. 3NF Decomposition Employee ( Emp_ID , Emp_Name, Dept_ID ) Department ( Dept_ID , Dept_Name, Dept_Location) Consider the relation R(Student, Subject, Teacher)

Analysis Candidate Keys: (Student, Subject) and (Student, Teacher) . For the FD Teacher → Subject , Teacher is a determinant but not a super key . Therefore, R violates BCNF. BCNF Decomposition Teach_Subj ( Teacher , Subject) Stud_Teach ( Student, Teacher ) Both tables are now strictly in BCNF. Given a relation R(A, B, C, D)

Candidate Keys {A, B} + = {A, B, C, D} {B, C} + = {A, B, C, D} (since C → D and D → A) {B, D} + = {A, B, C, D} (since D → A and AB → C) The candidate keys are AB, BC, and BD . All attributes are prime attributes except none (every attribute is part of at least one candidate key). Highest Normal Form Because there are no non-prime attributes, the relation is automatically in 3NF . However, check BCNF: The FD C → D has determinant C, which is not a super key. Thus, it violates BCNF. The highest normal form is 3NF .

Generalization, specialization and aggregation in the Extended E-R model

Specialization (Top-Down) The process of defining a set of subclasses from an entity type based on distinguishing characteristics. Example: An Employee can be specialized into Hourly_Emp and Salaried_Emp . Generalization (Bottom-Up) The reverse of specialization. Extracting shared characteristics from multiple entity types to create a generalized superclass. Example: Car and Truck generalized into Vehicle . Aggregation Treating a relationship between entities as a single abstract entity, allowing relationships to participate in other relationships. Example: A Project and Employee have a Works_On relationship. A Manager manages the entire Works_On relationship, treating it as one aggregated entity. Decomposition Decomposition is the process of breaking down a large, poorly-designed relation into two or more smaller relations to eliminate redundancy and anomalies.

Lossless-Join Decomposition A decomposition of R into R1 and R2 is lossless if joining R1 and R2 back together using a Natural Join yields the exact original relation R, without generating spurious (fake) tuples. Condition: The common attributes must be a candidate key for at least one of the decomposed relations (i.e., R1 ∩ R2 → R1 or R1 ∩ R2 → R2 ). Dependency-Preserving Decomposition A decomposition is dependency-preserving if all original functional dependencies can be checked and enforced using only the decomposed relations, without needing to join them back together. How is decomposition related to normalization Normalization uses Decomposition as its primary mechanism. When a relation violates a normal form, we decompose it into smaller relations that satisfy the normal form.

Example Suppose a relation R(EmpID, EmpName, DeptID, DeptName) where EmpID → EmpName, DeptID and DeptID → DeptName . This violates 3NF due to the transitive dependency ( EmpID → DeptID → DeptName ). Normalization Process: We decompose R into two relations to remove the redundancy: 1. Employee(EmpID, EmpName, DeptID) 2. Department(DeptID, DeptName) This decomposition is both lossless-join (because DeptID is a primary key in Department) and dependency-preserving. Transaction A transaction is a logical unit of work consisting of one or more SQL statements that must be executed entirely

or not at all. ACID Properties (Bank Transfer Example: A to B): Atomicity : "All or nothing." If money is deducted from A, it MUST be credited to B. If either fails, the entire transaction is rolled back. Consistency : The database must remain in a valid state. The total sum of A + B's balances must be the same before and after the transaction. Isolation : Concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other. If another transaction reads A's balance during the transfer, it will see the state either strictly before or strictly after, not midway. Durability : Once the transaction is committed, the changes are permanent and will survive system crashes. Transaction State Diagram COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT COMMIT : Saves all changes made during the current transaction permanently. ROLLBACK : Undoes all changes made during the current transaction, reverting to the last commit. SAVEPOINT : Sets a marker within a transaction so you can roll back to that specific point without canceling the entire transaction. START TRANSACTION; UPDATE ACCOUNT SET Balance = Balance - 500 WHERE Acc_No = 'A101'; SAVEPOINT step1; UPDATE ACCOUNT SET Balance = Balance + 500 WHERE Acc_No = 'A102'; -- If something goes

wrong here: ROLLBACK TO step1; -- Undoes only the A102 update COMMIT; -- Saves the final state Write a transaction that transfers Rs START TRANSACTION; SAVEPOINT before_transfer; UPDATE ACCOUNT SET Balance = Balance - 3000 WHERE Acc_No = 'A102'; UPDATE ACCOUNT SET Balance = Balance + 3000 WHERE Acc_No = 'A103'; COMMIT; Using a searched CASE statement, classify each account's Balance as 'High' if it is 25000 or more, 'Medium' if it is 15000 or more, and 'Low' otherwise SELECT Acc_No, Name, Balance, CASE WHEN Balance >= 25000 THEN 'High' WHEN Balance >= 15000 THEN 'Medium' ELSE 'Low' END AS Balance_Category FROM ACCOUNT; Write a query SELECT Acc_No, Name, Balance, IF(Balance < 15000, 'Low Balance Alert', 'OK') AS Status FROM ACCOUNT; Write a query SELECT Acc_No, Name, COALESCE(Nominee_Name, 'Not Registered') AS Nominee FROM ACCOUNT; In one or two lines each, state the purpose of a stored procedure, a sequence (AUTO_INCREMENT in MySQL), a cursor and a trigger Stored Procedure : A pre-compiled collection of SQL statements saved in the database that can be executed as a single callable routine. Sequence (AUTO_INCREMENT) : Automatically generates unique, sequential numeric values, typically used for primary keys. Cursor : A database object used to

retrieve and process rows one by one from a result set inside a stored procedure. Trigger : A special type of stored procedure that automatically executes (fires) in response to specific DML events (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) on a table. BEFORE trigger and an AFTER trigger BEFORE Trigger executes before the triggering DML operation is applied (useful for validation/modification of incoming data). AFTER Trigger executes after the operation (useful for auditing or cascading changes to other tables). NEW refers to the incoming data (being inserted or updated). OLD refers to the existing data in the table before the operation (being updated or deleted). Purpose of exception handling in a stored procedure Exception handling ensures that if an error occurs during execution, the stored procedure can catch it and gracefully handle it (e.g., rolling back a transaction) instead of crashing. DECLARE ... HANDLER : Defines a block of code to execute when a specific error or condition occurs (e.g., DECLARE CONTINUE HANDLER FOR SQLEXCEPTION ). SIGNAL : Used to artificially raise a custom error or exception, returning a custom SQLSTATE and message to the caller.
